26:1.text: And profited in the Jews’ religion above many my equals in mine own nation, being more exceedingly zealous of the traditions of my fathers.

provenance.other: “traditions of my fathers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Galatians 1:14. The KJV otherwise puts the word in a hostile setting — the tradition of the elders, the tradition of men (Matthew 15, Mark 7, Colossians 2:8) — and never once approves of it.
provenance.alternative: 1 Peter 1:18, ‘vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers’, which is the other place the KJV joins tradition to ancestors; but it inverts the possessive and, like the Gospel occurrences, condemns what it names.
provenance.significance: The KJV has no positive sense of the phrase, and Mosiah 26:1 needs one: here the tradition of the fathers is the true religion and refusing it is the sin. So the narrator has taken the diction of Paul's pre-conversion zeal and reversed its polarity — Paul's ‘traditions of my fathers’ is what he had to be knocked off a horse to abandon, and Mosiah's is what the rising generation are damned for abandoning. That reversal is worth holding for one chapter: the very next chapter puts one of these unbelievers on the road with a heavenly voice and a three-day collapse, and the man who gets up is called to bear the name he had blasphemed.

26:1.note: ‘They did not believe the tradition of their fathers.’ The construction — tradition, possessive, fathers — is Galatians 1:14's and nowhere else's in the KJV, and the chapter's larger interest in a generation that will not receive what was handed down runs through Mosiah 26 to Alma the Younger's conversion in 27. The link is moderate rather than high because the three words are the whole of the contact and the idea of ancestral tradition needs no source; what recommends it is that English scripture supplies exactly one shape for the phrase and this is it.

26:6.text: For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness:

provenance.other: “flattering words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 2:5. The nearest relatives are Psalm 12:2-3's ‘flattering lips’, a different noun in a different construction.
provenance.significance: 1 Thessalonians 2:5 is Paul distinguishing true preaching from false: the apostle who did not use flattering words is set against those who do, and the whole paragraph is about what a minister owes the congregation he gathered. Mosiah 26:6 borrows the phrase for exactly the people Paul is contrasting himself with — dissenters ‘which were in the church’, working from inside it — and the verse that follows sets up the church's disciplinary machinery as the answer. The catalogue's interest is that the Book of Mormon reaches for the one KJV phrase that names the offence in a specifically pastoral register, not a merely political one.

26:6.note: ‘They did deceive many with their flattering words, which were in the church.’ Deceit by speech is a universal idea; ‘flattering words’ is not — it is one verse of the KJV, and it is a verse about ministry corrupted from within, which is precisely Mosiah 26:6's subject. The link is high rather than certain because two words cannot be quotation, but the singleton and the coinciding setting do the work together.

26:11.text: Then said Pilate unto them, Take ye him, and judge him according to your law. The Jews therefore said unto him, It is not lawful for us to put any man to death:

provenance.other: “judge him according to” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 18:31, and “according to your law” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The whole formula — a ruler telling accusers to take the accused and judge them by their own standard — exists once in English scripture.
provenance.significance: Read the two verses together and Mosiah 26:11-12 is John 18:29-31 with the jurisdictions exchanged. In John the religious court brings the accused to the civil ruler and the ruler hands them back: ‘Take ye him, and judge him according to your law.’ In Mosiah the high priest brings the accused to the king and the king hands them back: ‘I judge them not; therefore I deliver them into thy hands to be judged.’ The Jews' reply in John is the reason the remand fails — ‘it is not lawful for us to put any man to death’ — and it is exactly the limit Alma does not have, because Mosiah has already given him ‘the authority over the church’ (26:8). So the passage that founds Nephite church discipline is built on the passage where a civil ruler washes his hands of a religious charge, and it removes the one clause that made Pilate's remand impossible. Nothing in Mosiah says this; the borrowed formula says it.

26:11.note: ‘Therefore we have brought them before thee, that thou may judge them according to their crimes.’ Both halves of the KJV's one occurrence of this remand formula are here across two verses, with ‘law’ replaced by ‘crimes’ — which is the substitution the situation requires, since Alma has no written law to judge by and goes to God for one in 26:13. The 1830 ‘may judge’ (1920 ‘mayest’) leaves the second person less marked than the KJV's, but the verb, the preposition and the sequence are John's. Catalogued at 26:11, where the verbal contact sits; the remand itself is 26:12.

26:14.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

provenance.other: “poured out his soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 53:12, and “poured out my soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 1:15. Mosiah 26:14 has the third-person form, which is Isaiah's; Hannah's is first-person and past-continuous.
provenance.alternative: 1 Samuel 1:15, Hannah at Shiloh, which matches the situation — a distressed private prayer at a sanctuary answered by a priest — better than it matches the wording. Kept as a composite rather than the source because the grammar is Isaiah's.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's quietest and best-motivated borrowing. Isaiah 53:12 is transcribed whole into this same book at Mosiah 14:12, in Abinadi's mouth, and Mosiah 26:15 names Abinadi one verse later as the man whose words Alma believed. So Alma prays in the words of the chapter that converted him. Recover the rest of Isaiah 53:12 and the fit tightens: the servant ‘poured out his soul’, ‘was numbered with the transgressors’, and ‘made intercession for the transgressors’. Alma pours out his soul (26:14) over what to do about the transgressor (26:19), and the sentence he is given turns on who shall and shall not be ‘numbered among my people’ (26:32, 26:36). Three of Isaiah 53:12's four clauses are doing work in this chapter, and the one that is not — dividing the spoil — is the one with no bearing on a disciplinary case.

26:14.note: ‘After he had poured out his whole soul to God.’ The KJV pours out a soul twice, and Mosiah 26:14 has Isaiah's person and tense with ‘whole’ inserted. What settles the route is not the wording but the neighbourhood: this book already contains Isaiah 53 verbatim at Mosiah 14, spoken by the prophet Alma is about to be praised for believing, and the chapter goes on to use two more of that verse's clauses — intercession for the transgressor, and being numbered or not numbered among a people. Mediation is recorded as OT-via-earlier-BoM on that ground; the wording alone cannot decide it, since Mosiah 14:12 and Isaiah 53:12 are identical at every word Mosiah 26:14 reproduces.

26:15.text: And Jesus answered and said unto him, Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven.

provenance.other: “Blessed art thou” occurs in exactly five KJV verses. Three address the LORD, a land, or a woman among women; only Matthew 16:17 opens with the formula and then names a man — ‘Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona’ — which is the shape Mosiah 26:15 has: ‘Blessed art thou, Alma’.
provenance.significance: Matthew 16:17-19 is one speech in three moves: a man is blessed by name, is told a church will be built, and is handed the power to bind and loose. Mosiah 26 makes the same three moves in the same order and over eleven verses — ‘Blessed art thou, Alma’ (15), ‘thou hast established a church among this people’ (17), and then the reciprocal formula that governs the rest of the chapter, ‘him shall ye receive into the church; and him will I also receive’ (21) against ‘the same shall ye not receive into my church, for him I will not receive at the last day’ (28). That last pair is the binding-and-loosing of Matthew 16:19 with the earth-and-heaven axis rewritten as now-and-the-last-day. The Book of Mormon is not quoting the Petrine commission; it is running its structure, and it is running it over the founder of a church rather than over an apostle.

26:15.note: The voice from heaven blesses a named man, credits him with a church, and gives him a ratified power to admit and exclude. That is the sequence of Matthew 16:17-19 and there is no other KJV passage with it. The verbal contact at 26:15 itself is only the four-word address, one of five KJV occurrences and the only one to name a man — so the argument rests on the sequence and on the reciprocal receive/receive-not formula it produces at 26:21 and 26:28, which is Matthew 16:19's construction with a different pair of realms. High rather than certain because no clause is reproduced whole.

26:18.text: But the Lord said unto him, Go thy way: for he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel:

provenance.other: “bear my name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 9:15. Bearing a name in the KJV is otherwise done by the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28), never by a people.
provenance.significance: Acts 9:15 is the Lord's answer to Ananias about the newly blinded Saul, and it is the KJV's only sentence about a person appointed to bear the divine name. Mosiah 26:18-20 gives that appointment to a whole people and then, two verses on, to Alma personally — ‘thou art my servant … go forth in my name’. The chapter after this one stages a persecutor struck down by a heavenly voice, laid out speechless for days, and raised up to preach the faith he had been destroying; that Mosiah 26 has already borrowed the sentence the Lord speaks about Saul between his blinding and his rising is the sort of thing this catalogue exists to notice.

26:18.note: ‘Blessed is this people, which is willing to bear my name.’ Two of the three words are common and the third is not: the KJV lets exactly one person bear the divine name, and he is Saul of Tarsus three days after the Damascus road. Moderate rather than high because ‘bear my name’ is short enough to be reinvented, and because Mosiah has transferred it from an individual commission to a corporate one; what keeps it worth writing is Acts 9:15's position in a narrative Mosiah 27 is about to reproduce. Note also that the 1830 ‘this people, which is willing’ preserves the singular verb that 1920 corrected to ‘are’.

26:21.text: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:

provenance.other: “hear my voice” occurs in exactly 11 KJV verses and “my sheep” in exactly 10; the two meet in exactly 2 verses, John 10:16 and John 10:27, both in the good-shepherd discourse. Ezekiel 34, the other great my-sheep chapter, never joins them.
provenance.alternative: Ezekiel 34:11-12, which supplies ‘gather together my sheep’ at 26:20 more directly than John does; but Ezekiel's sheep are sought, not self-selected by hearing, and the conditional at 26:21 is John's move.
provenance.significance: John 10:27 states a fact about sheep — they hear. Mosiah 26:21 turns it into an entrance requirement: ‘he that will hear my voice, shall be my sheep.’ The predication runs the other way, and that reversal is the whole administrative point of the chapter, because it converts a description of the flock into a test the church can apply at the door. John 10:16's ‘other sheep I have, which are not of this fold … they shall hear my voice’ is the verse Latter-day Saint reading has long taken to point at this hemisphere, so the discourse being mined here is one the Book of Mormon has an interest in; but what 26:21 actually does with it is procedural, not prophetic.

26:21.note: ‘And he that will hear my voice, shall be my sheep.’ Both content phrases come from the two KJV verses that hold them together, and 26:28's negative — ‘he that will not hear my voice, the same shall ye not receive’ — completes the conversion of John's description into a rule of admission. The immediately preceding clause, ‘gather together my sheep’ (26:20), is Ezekiel 34's idiom rather than John's, so the discourse is composite; the link is filed at 26:21 because that is where the wording is decisive.

26:23.text: The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.

provenance.other: “taketh away the sin of the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:29. The KJV never elsewhere says that anyone takes sin, in either direction, with the world as its object.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 26:23 changes two words of the KJV's one formula and both changes matter: away becomes upon, and sin becomes sins. John's Lamb removes the world's sin from it; Mosiah's speaker loads it onto himself. That is the difference between an expiation described from outside and one described by the victim in the first person, which is what the whole verse is doing — ‘it is I that taketh … it is I that hath created … it is I that granteth’. The borrowed clause is being said by the Lamb rather than about him, and the preposition is what carries the change.

26:23.note: ‘For it is I that taketh upon me the sins of the world.’ The Baptist's formula, in the first person, with the preposition reversed. Its rarity is absolute — one KJV verse — and the substitution of ‘upon me’ for ‘away’ is too pointed to be accidental in a chapter whose subject is who bears whose sins. The same source stands behind 1 Nephi 10:10, where the Baptist's own words are given to Lehi.

26:23.text: And he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left.

provenance.other: ‘Right hand’ is far too common in the KJV to identify a source by itself — 164 verses. What is not common is the collocation this chapter builds: sheep who hear a voice, a place at a right hand, a second summons for those the judge never knew, and a sentence to everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels. Matthew 25:31-46 is the only KJV passage with all four.
provenance.significance: The verbatim hit in this chapter is at 26:27, four verses further on. Filing a moderate link here records where the discourse actually starts running Matthew 25 — at the sheep of 26:21 and the right hand of 26:23-24 — so that the quotation at 26:27 reads as the end of a sustained borrowing rather than a stray. Matthew 25:33 sets sheep at a right hand; Mosiah 26:21-24 makes one his sheep and gives him a place at that right hand, and then 26:25-27 turns to the ones on the other side.

26:23.note: ‘A place at my right hand’, said four verses after the sheep of 26:21 and four verses before the left-hand sentence of Matthew 25:41 is quoted outright at 26:27. Taken alone the phrase proves nothing; taken as the middle term of that sequence it shows the sheep-and-goats judgment being worked through in order. Moderate, and kjvSpecific ‘uncertain’, because no phrase here is distinctive enough to test — the evidence is the ordering, not the wording.

26:25.text: In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.

provenance.other: “last trump” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the trumpet shall sound” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both 1 Corinthians 15:52. ‘Second trump’ occurs in no KJV verse at all; the KJV numbers no trumpets outside Revelation's series of seven, and never with an ordinal attached to ‘trump’.
provenance.significance: A ‘second trump’ is only intelligible against a scheme in which trumps are counted, and the KJV's one counted trump is Paul's last one. Mosiah 26:25 assumes a first trump it never mentions — at which, on the logic of 26:24, those who know him come forth — and puts the strangers at the second. So the verse quietly makes Paul's terminal blast into a penultimate one, and the resurrection of the righteous and the resurrection of those who never knew him into two separately trumpeted events. The doctrine that follows from that ordering is developed at length later in the Book of Mormon; the vocabulary that makes it sayable is Paul's.

26:25.note: ‘When the second trump shall sound.’ The verb and its subject are 1 Corinthians 15:52's, which is the KJV's only sounding trumpet of the resurrection, and the ordinal is not the KJV's at all. Recorded as an echo at moderate confidence: the wording is too short to demonstrate dependence, but ‘second trump’ is a coinage that needs a numbered series to lean against and Paul's ‘last trump’ is the only one English scripture offers.

26:27.text: Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:

provenance.other: “everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:41. ‘Everlasting fire’ itself occurs in two, both in Matthew.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 26:27 keeps the sentence and changes the grammar of its delivery. In Matthew the Son of man says ‘Depart from me’ and the goats go; in Mosiah the ones addressed ‘shall depart into everlasting fire’ — reported rather than commanded. What is preserved exactly is the clause that gives the fire its history: it was not made for them. Matthew 25:41 is the KJV's only statement that hell was prepared for someone other than the human beings sent there, and the chapter that has spent ten verses telling Alma whom to receive ends its warning on the one verse that says the place of exclusion was built for another tenant.

26:27.note: A ten-word verbatim run, and the phrase is a KJV singleton. This falls below Skousen's sixteen-word operational threshold and is not one of his thirty-six extended passages; it is catalogued as a quotation because the clause is complete, unmistakable, and reproduced without variation (CONVENTIONS §2). The 1830 ‘then will I confess’ was reordered to ‘then I will confess’ in 1920, which moves the verse away from its other source, Matthew 7:23 — see the second link at this verse.

26:27.text: And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.

provenance.route: Matthew 7:23 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with the verb drawn from Matthew 10:32
provenance.other: “then will I profess unto them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “I never knew you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both Matthew 7:23. “him will I confess” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 10:32.
provenance.significance: The 1830 text reads ‘And then will I confess unto them, that I never knew them’ against Matthew 7:23's ‘And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you’. Every word is the KJV's except the verb and the two pronouns, and the pronouns follow from the change of address — Matthew's judge speaks to the condemned, Mosiah's speaks about them to Alma. The verb is the interesting substitution, because the KJV's other word for this judicial act is ‘confess’, and it uses it in exactly one place: Matthew 10:32, where whoever confesses Christ before men is confessed before the Father. So Mosiah 26:27 sets the two halves of that promise against each other in one sentence: the act that is elsewhere the acknowledging of the faithful is here the formal disowning of the strangers. 1920's reordering to ‘then I will confess’ breaks the KJV's word order and makes the borrowing harder to see, which is why 1830 is the running text.

26:27.note: Matthew 7:23 and Matthew 25:41 are the two KJV verses of final rejection and this one sentence uses both — the first for its opening clause, the second for its close. The 1830 reading preserves Matthew's inversion, ‘then will I’, which 1920 normalized; and ‘confess’ for ‘profess’ is not a slip but the KJV's own alternative verb for the same act at Matthew 10:32, the only place it occurs in this construction. High rather than certain only because one word of the seven-word opening differs.

26:30.text: And if he trespass against thee seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turn again to thee, saying, I repent; thou shalt forgive him.

provenance.other: “seven times in a day” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 17:4, which is also the KJV's only place where a repentant offender is quoted saying ‘I repent’ as the trigger for an obligation to forgive.
provenance.significance: Luke 17:3-4 is the KJV's only forgiveness rule with all three of Mosiah 26:29-31's parts: a brother who trespasses, a rebuke, and an obligation to forgive that is renewed every time the offender says he repents. Mosiah replaces the numeral with an adverb — ‘as often as my people repent’ for ‘seven times in a day’ — which is the same generalization Matthew 18:22 performs on the same rule with ‘seventy times seven’. What Mosiah 26 adds is a second party: in Luke the forgiveness is horizontal, between brothers, and here it is doubled, ‘him shall ye forgive, and I will forgive him also’, so that the church's act and God's are made to track each other. That doubling is Matthew 16:19's, and it is what turns Luke's counsel into a procedure.

26:30.note: ‘As often as my people repent, will I forgive them their trespasses against me’ (26:30), and ‘when he saith that he repenteth’ (26:31), are Luke 17:3-4's two conditions in Luke's order, with the numeral generalized. ‘Trespass against thee’ is Luke's verb and Mosiah has it twice, at 26:29 and 26:30. The 1830 ‘saith that he repenteth’ keeps the KJV's present tense where 1920 has ‘says that he repents’, which is a small instance of the pattern noted at CONVENTIONS §8. Filed at 26:30 because that is where the generalization is made.

26:31.text: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

provenance.other: “your trespasses” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 6:15, Mark 11:25 and Mark 11:26 — and all three are the same saying. ‘Forgive one another’ occurs in no KJV verse; the KJV's idiom is ‘forgiving one another’ (Ephesians 4:32, Colossians 3:13), which Mosiah has conjugated into an imperative.
provenance.significance: Matthew 6:15 makes the failure to forgive cost the unforgiving man his own pardon. Mosiah 26:31 makes it cost him something narrower and more legal — ‘the same hath brought himself under condemnation’ — which is not a KJV phrase at all, and which relocates the penalty from the Father's decision to the offender's own act. The chapter is converting sayings into statutes throughout; this is the clearest single case, because the source states a consequence and the borrowing states a liability.

26:31.note: ‘Ye shall also forgive one another your trespasses … He that forgiveth not his neighbor's trespasses.’ The noun is Matthew 6:15's — three KJV verses have it, all one saying — and the second clause reproduces its conditional shape. Moderate rather than high because the language of forgiving trespasses is spread across Matthew 6, Matthew 18:35 and Mark 11, and no one of them is decisively in view; what is in view is the saying they all carry.

26:36.text: He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels.

provenance.other: “blot out his name” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 29:20 and Revelation 3:5. Deuteronomy blots the name from under heaven as a curse; Revelation 3:5 promises the overcomer that his name will not be blotted from the book of life.
provenance.significance: Revelation 3:5 is the only KJV verse that holds this chapter's two administrative acts together: not blotting a name out, and confessing a name before the Father. Mosiah 26 performs both, in reverse order and with the polarity flipped — the Lord confesses to the strangers that he never knew them (26:27), and the unrepentant have their names blotted out (26:36). Read against Revelation, Alma's register is the negative image of the book of life: what the church strikes from its roll is what heaven promises the faithful will never lose, and the confession Revelation makes a reward is here made a sentence.

26:36.note: ‘Their names were blotted out.’ Two KJV verses blot out a name and only one of them is about church membership. The link is moderate and conceptual — Mosiah shares no clause with Revelation 3:5 — but the pairing of a struck name with a confessed name is distinctive enough to be worth recording, and Mosiah 26 has both, nine verses apart. That the record Alma keeps is a physical one he ‘wrote down’ (26:33) makes the analogy to a book with names in it exact rather than metaphorical.

26:37.text: See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,

provenance.other: “circumspectly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 5:15, and its collocation with the verb walk is that verse's whole point. The word is otherwise absent from English scripture.
provenance.significance: Ephesians 5:15-16 tells a congregation to walk circumspectly and to redeem the time ‘because the days are evil’. Mosiah 26:37 uses the phrase for a church that has just come through a disciplinary crisis and is prospering again — walking circumspectly before God, receiving many, baptizing many. The borrowed adverb carries the reason with it: circumspection is what Ephesians prescribes for a community surrounded by danger, and Mosiah 26:38 immediately supplies the danger, ‘being persecuted by all those who did not belong to the church of God’.

26:37.note: A single word, but one that exists in exactly one KJV verse and appears here in the same construction as there. Verses 37 and 38 together reproduce Ephesians 5:15-16's pairing of circumspect walking with an evil surrounding age, which is what raises this above a lexical coincidence.

provenance.other: “pray without ceasing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 5:17, and “in every thing give thanks” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Thessalonians 5:18. They are consecutive.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 26:39 takes two consecutive KJV verses in their KJV order and joins them with ‘and’: ‘being commanded of God to pray without ceasing, and to give thanks in all things’. The second is loosened — 1830 has ‘in all things’ where Paul has ‘in every thing’ — but the pairing is not available anywhere else in English scripture, and it is a pairing rather than a single phrase, which is what makes the borrowing demonstrable rather than lexical. The chapter that opened with a church having to invent a disciplinary procedure ends by putting its officers under the shortest two commandments Paul ever wrote.

26:39.note: Three words, reproduced whole, from a verse that is only three words long — one of the KJV's shortest — followed immediately by a paraphrase of the verse that follows it. Catalogued as a quotation on the completeness of the clause rather than its length, and well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold (CONVENTIONS §2). The looser second half, ‘in all things’ for ‘in every thing’, is the mark of a writer working from memory of the pair rather than copying it.
